newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish c.bank acts to curb dollar demand-bankers.
newsitem.headline: Turkish c.bank acts to curb dollar demand-bankers.

text.p: The Turkish central bank allowed overnight money and repo rates to soar on Tuesday to curb rising dollar demand due to political uncertainty, bankers said.

They said the market, already haunted by turmoil over the fate of the Islamist-led coalition and the possibility of early polls, was destabilised after many banks were unable to square their lira positions late on Monday because state banks did not repay their overnight borrowing on time.
They said the central bank did not provide its usual funding to state banks for heavy mid-month public sector salary payments late on Monday, causing the market to fall extremely short.
"The central bank is acting to control the foreign currency rates by further tightening the liquidity," said one banker.

The money market opened 34.6 trillion lira short on Tuesday. The average overnight repo rate jumped to 86.2 percent from Monday's 78.61 while banks' overnight bids on the over-the-counter (OTC) money market leapt to 87 percent from around 80 percent on Monday.

The average overnight rate on the screen-based interbank where the central bank began lending cash at 72 percent from the opening, was unchanged at 71.98 percent. Banks' borrowing on this central-bank brokered market are limited to their lines.

"It looks as though the central bank began acting on its own (to control the markets), independently from the government. This further raised suspicions that the coalition would not last," said another private banker.
"But the central bank's move is correct although belated," he added.
Bankers said demand in the Treasury's inflation-indexed, two-year bond auction would be extremely low amid political uncertainty and sharply higher overnight funding costs.
"Demand in the auction will be very low and any bids that come will be at flier risk premiums," said one banker.

The risk premium had leapt to 32 percent from previous 29.95 percent on political worries in the last auction on June 3 when the Treasury sold 198.1 trillion lira of the two-year, inflation-indexed bonds.
Bankers have long been complaining that trade in these bonds was very weak because of the funding risks involved in buying such long-term papers amid political concerns.
But the Treasury has insisted on issuing these instruments in the last six auctions held since the beginning of April.

"In an environment where the future of the government is unknown, an alteration in the prime ministry is imminent and funding costs have jumped to almost 90 percent levels, there is no logic in buying papers," said one banker.
The lira stood at 145,650 at midday, slightly easier than Monday's 145,400 close, in line with the dollar/mark parity and the overnight funding cost, bankers said.
The central bank had bought lira for dollars just before the close on Monday after the lira weakened to 145,500 to curb fresh dollar demand buoyed by political turmoil.

It also funded heavily on the interbank on Monday by lending banks 40.2 trillion lira at 72 percent on overnight, 26.9 trillion lira at 69 percent via tmrw/next and 7.5 trillion lira at 70 percent via tmrw/next.
Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller said on Monday Islamist PM Necmettin Erbakan would resign in the next couple of days to hand power over to her in the run-up to snap polls.
A spokesman from Erbakan's Islamist Welfare Party also said on Monday they had conditionally agreed to hand over power to their pro-Western coalition ally True Path Party later this week.

Ciller and Erbakan had announced on June 1 that they would seek early elections with a caretaker government to be headed by Ciller to overcome a row between the government and the secularist army over religious activism.
However, the coalition now has 274 seats in the 550-member parliament and relies on support from a small rightist party to pass an alteration in government and an early election law.
